subject: Agriculture
title: Carbon Farming
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Carbon Farming.

hook.text: Soil holds three times more carbon than the atmosphere. Farming practices could turn cropland into a massive carbon sink.

buildup.text: Cover crops, no-till, and compost application increase soil organic carbon—pulling CO₂ from the air into the ground.

discovery.text: Carbon credit markets pay farmers $15–30 per ton of CO₂ sequestered. A new revenue stream from healthy soil.

twist.text: Measuring soil carbon accurately is hard and expensive. Verification challenges slow the market's growth.

climax.text: If global cropland increased soil carbon by 0.4% per year, it could offset all human CO₂ emissions. It's called 4 per 1000.

punchline.text: Pay farmers to store carbon. The soil is the cheapest carbon capture machine on Earth.

quiz.question: How much more carbon does soil hold compared to the atmosphere?

details.summary: Carbon farming uses agricultural practices that capture atmospheric carbon and store it in soil and vegetation. This topic covers cover cropping, reduced tillage, agroforestry, and how carbon credit markets incentivize farmers to sequester greenhouse gases.
details.whyItMatters: Agriculture contributes about 10% of global emissions but has the potential to become a net carbon sink. Carbon farming turns climate action into a revenue stream for farmers.
takeaways: Healthy soils can store two to three times more carbon than the atmosphere
No-till and cover cropping are the most accessible carbon farming practices
Carbon credit markets pay farmers $15–50 per ton of verified CO₂ sequestered

faq.question: What is carbon farming and how does it work?
faq.answer: Carbon farming uses practices like cover cropping, no-till, composting, and agroforestry to increase the amount of carbon dioxide captured from the atmosphere and stored as organic carbon in soils and perennial plant biomass.

faq.question: Can farmers earn money from carbon farming?
faq.answer: Yes. Voluntary carbon credit markets and government programs pay farmers for verified carbon sequestration. Payments typically range from $15 to $50 per ton of CO₂ equivalent, creating a new income stream alongside crop production.
